summary: This document defines additional MODP Diffie-Hellman groups for SSH that use SHA-2 hashes. It also updates RFC 4250 and updates RFC 4253 by correcting an error about checking the peer's Diffie-Hellman public key.

plainLanguage.summary: When a Secure Shell connection starts, the two ends agree a shared secret without sending it, using a Diffie-Hellman exchange over a large prime number. This RFC adds five names for that exchange, using bigger primes and a stronger hash function than the ones Secure Shell defined first. It also fixes a small but real mistake in the original rules about which values of the other end's public key are acceptable.

subtitle: Newer Diffie-Hellman groups for Secure Shell, and a correction to the range check on the peer's key.

tldr.problem: Secure Shell had key exchange methods built on SHA-1 and on a 2048-bit Diffie-Hellman group. Guidance for systems handling classified national security information says those should no longer be used, and that the Diffie-Hellman prime modulus should be at least 3072 bits.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers five new key exchange method names: diffie-hellman-group14-sha256, and diffie-hellman-group15-sha512 through diffie-hellman-group18-sha512, using the group sizes already defined for Internet Key Exchange. It also corrects an error in RFC 4253, which stated the acceptable range of the peer's public key as closed rather than open.
tldr.outcome: SSH implementations have standard names to negotiate for larger groups with a stronger hash, and the corrected check keeps the peer's public value out of the two-element subgroup. The RFC also repeats the warning that fixed Diffie-Hellman parameters make an attractive target for pre-computation.

facts.label: New key exchange methods
facts.value: 5 names: group14 with SHA-256 and groups 15 to 18 with SHA-512

facts.label: Minimum modulus in the guidance
facts.value: a Diffie-Hellman prime modulus of at least 3072 bits

today: RFC 8268 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2017. It updates RFC 4250 and RFC 4253, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or further updates it. The group sizes it names come from RFC 3526.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
The Diffie-Hellman key exchange used by Secure Shell negotiates a shared secret without sending it across the network, by exchanging public values and applying a modular exponentiation with a large prime modulus. This document defines added Modular Exponentiation (MODP) groups for Secure Shell using SHA-2 hashes. It updates RFC 4250, the registry of Secure Shell assigned numbers, and updates RFC 4253 by correcting an error about checking the peer's Diffie-Hellman public key. It is intended that these new MODP groups with SHA-2-based hashes update Section 6.4 of RFC 4253 and Section 4.10 of RFC 4250.

The 2048-bit MODP group 14 is already present in most SSH implementations, and most implementations already have a SHA256 implementation, so diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 is provided as the easy one to implement. The larger groups are provided for deployments that need them.
sections.plainLanguage: Secure Shell already had a way to agree a shared secret. This RFC gives it five more ways, with bigger numbers and a newer hash, and fixes a mistake in the rules for checking what the other end sends.

sections.title: Why Newer Groups and Hashes
sections.content:
The United States Information Assurance Directorate at the National Security Agency has published a frequently-asked-questions document on the Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite and quantum computing, addressed to organizations that run classified or unclassified national security systems and to vendors who build products used in them. That document indicates that such systems should no longer use elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curve digital signatures with NIST P-256, nor SHA-256, nor AES-128, nor RSA with 2048-bit keys, nor Diffie-Hellman with 2048-bit keys. For SSH that means avoiding the ecdh-sha2-nistp256 and ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 algorithms, avoiding any key exchange method that uses SHA1, SHA224 or SHA256 in favour of SHA384 or SHA512, avoiding the aes128-cbc and aes128-ctr encryption algorithms, and avoiding ssh-rsa with SHA1 as well as x509v3-rsa2048-sha256 and any other RSA key shorter than 3072 bits or using a hash weaker than SHA384. It also advises against both diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 and diffie-hellman-group14-sha1, and against diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 added by this document.

The same guidance says users should select Diffie-Hellman groups based on well-established and validated parameter sets that meet the minimum required sizes: elliptic curves are restricted to the NIST P-384 group for both Diffie-Hellman and signatures, RSA moduli should be at least 3072 bits other than the noted public key infrastructure exception, and for Diffie-Hellman a prime modulus of at least 3072 bits should be used, which for the bit sizes specified in RFC 3526 allows any of group15, group16, group17 or group18.

Although SSH may not always be used to protect Top Secret communications, this document adopts the groups given as an example in that guidance, and adopts SHA512 rather than SHA256 for the new groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Government guidance for systems handling classified information says that 2048-bit Diffie-Hellman and SHA-256 should no longer be used, and that the prime at the heart of the exchange should be at least 3072 bits. This RFC supplies names for the groups that meet that bar.

sections.title: The New Key Exchange Method Names
sections.content:
This document adds five new Key Exchange Algorithm Method Names to those originally defined in RFC 4253 and RFC 4250, and adopts the style and conventions of RFC 4253 in specifying how the use of new data key exchange is indicated in SSH. The names are diffie-hellman-group14-sha256, diffie-hellman-group15-sha512, diffie-hellman-group16-sha512, diffie-hellman-group17-sha512 and diffie-hellman-group18-sha512. The SHA-2 family of secure hash algorithms is defined in RFC 6234, and SHA512 is to be used whenever sha512 appears in a key exchange method name.

The method of key exchange used for diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 is the same as that for diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 except that the SHA256 hash algorithm is used, and it is recommended that diffie-hellman-group14-sha256 SHOULD be supported to smooth the transition to newer group sizes. The group15 to group18 names are the same as those specified in RFC 3526: a 3072-bit MODP group15, a 4096-bit MODP group16, a 6144-bit MODP group17 and an 8192-bit MODP group18. IANA has added all five names to the Key Exchange Method Names registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Each name says two things: which prime group the exchange uses, and which hash function turns the exchange into a key. The first new name reuses the familiar 2048-bit group with SHA-256, which is the easy step. The other four use groups of 3072, 4096, 6144 and 8192 bits with SHA-512.

sections.title: Checking the Peer's Diffie-Hellman Public Key
sections.content:
Section 8 of RFC 4253 contains a small error in point 3. When checking the client's public value e and the server's public value f, it says that values of e or f that are not in the range [1, p-1] must not be sent or accepted by either side, and that if this condition is violated the key exchange fails. The problem is that the range should have been an open interval excluding the endpoint values.

This document amends that text. The peer's Diffie-Hellman public key values must be checked, and both conditions 1 < e < p-1 and 1 < f < p-1 must be true. Values not within those bounds must not be sent or accepted by either side, and if either condition is violated then the key exchange fails.

This simple check ensures that the remote peer behaves properly and that the local system is not forced into the two-element subgroup.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end sends a public value that must fall strictly between 1 and one less than the prime. The original rule allowed the two boundary values, which is wrong: the check now excludes them, so a value that would force the result into a tiny subgroup is refused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4253 apply to this document. The security considerations of RFC 3526 suggest that MODP group14 through group18 have security strengths that range between 110 bits of security through 310 bits of security, based on the method in RFC 3766. Care should be taken to use sufficient entropy and deterministic random-bit generator algorithms to maximize the true security strength of the key exchange and ciphers selected.

Using a fixed set of Diffie-Hellman parameters makes them a high value target for pre-computation. Generating additional sets of primes to be used, or moving to larger values, mitigates this issue.
sections.plainLanguage: The larger the group, the harder the exchange is to break, but a group that everybody uses can still be attacked by doing the hard work once in advance. Using several different groups, or a larger one, spreads that cost. The random numbers on each side matter too.

viz.caption: THE FIVE NEW KEY EXCHANGE METHOD NAMES

items.label: Group 14 with SHA-256
items.desc: The same exchange as diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 but with the SHA256 hash. The 2048-bit group is already in most SSH implementations and most already have SHA256, so this is the easy one to add.

items.label: Group 15 with SHA-512
items.desc: The 3072-bit MODP group15 with the SHA512 hash.

items.label: Group 16 with SHA-512
items.desc: The 4096-bit MODP group16 with the SHA512 hash.

items.label: Group 17 with SHA-512
items.desc: The 6144-bit MODP group17 with the SHA512 hash.

items.label: Group 18 with SHA-512
items.desc: The 8192-bit MODP group18 with the SHA512 hash.

data.title: Peer public key bounds
data.code:
1 < e < p-1
1 < f < p-1

e is the client public key, f is the server public key,
and p is the prime modulus of the MODP group.

Values outside those bounds must not be sent or
accepted by either side, and the key exchange fails
if either condition is violated.

viz.caption: WHAT THE RFC ASKS OPERATORS TO WATCH

items.title: 110 to 310 bits of security
items.text: The security considerations of RFC 3526 place MODP groups 14 through 18 in that range.

items.title: Fixed parameters are a target
items.text: A fixed set of Diffie-Hellman parameters makes it a high value target for pre-computation.

items.title: Generate more primes, or go larger
items.text: Generating additional sets of primes to be used, or moving to larger values, mitigates the pre-computation risk.

items.title: Entropy and randomness
items.text: Use sufficient entropy and good deterministic random-bit generator algorithms to reach the true security strength of the chosen key exchange and ciphers.
